rationale: ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanners, protocols and TR, and those differences show up as large site-specific shifts in the connectivity features. That shift is variance the classifier has to absorb, even though scoring is within-site. This change z-scores each connectivity edge within each acquisition site, using only that site's training subjects (and falling back to the global scaler for sites not seen in training). That removes site offsets and scale differences, so the regularized logistic regression can focus on ADHD-related connectivity differences within each site.

Scanners and protocols differ a lot between ADHD-200 sites, and the score is AUROC computed within each site. Standardizing every connectivity feature within its site, using training-fold mean and SD, removes site offsets from the pooled fit so the L2 logistic regression can focus on case-vs-control differences that hold inside each site.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, TR and scan length, so the shift in connectivity between sites is probably larger than the ADHD signal. The score is within-site AUROC, so I will z-score each connectivity feature within its own site (using training-fold statistics for that site) before the pooled L2-logistic model. The model can then learn directions that separate cases from controls within a site, not directions that separate sites.

I'm adding per-site harmonization: within each site, every connectivity feature is centred and scaled using that site's train and test subjects together. Site scanner and protocol effects are much larger than the ADHD signal, and the score is computed within site, so removing site-level shifts should let the L2 logistic regression focus on differences between subjects. The harmonization never uses labels. It also replaces the global StandardScaler, which the per-site scaling makes redundant.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner and protocol, and the score is computed within each site, so the classifier should only learn differences that hold inside a site. This change z-scores each connectivity feature per site (mean and SD from that site's training subjects) before the L2 logistic regression, so the model stops spending capacity on site offsets. If a test site has fewer than 5 training subjects, its stats come from its own test subjects instead, which uses no labels.

Scanner and protocol differences between the 8 ADHD-200 sites are large, and the score is AUROC computed within each site. So I'll z-score every connectivity feature within its own site (ComBat-style location/scale harmonization, using no labels) before the logistic regression. That way the model's limited capacity goes on differences between subjects, not between sites. Each site's statistics come from the train and test items of that site together, so a site that appears only in the test fold still gets harmonized.

This change z-scores every connectivity feature within its acquisition site, using labels-free per-site mean and standard deviation pooled over train and test. That stops the L2 logistic regression from spending its weights on site offsets and lets it focus on diagnosis-related variation inside each site.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol and TR, so a lot of the variance in the connectivity features comes from the site rather than from ADHD. The metric is AUROC computed within each site, so z-scoring each connectivity edge within each site removes that site offset and scale before the single regularized logistic regression is fit. Each site's mean and SD come from its training subjects; a site with fewer than 5 training subjects falls back to label-free statistics pooled from its train and test subjects.

I'm replacing the Fisher-z Pearson edges with a tangent-space embedding of the CC200 covariances. Each subject gets a Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance, which helps with the short and uneven scan lengths across sites. Each matrix is whitened by the group's log-Euclidean mean and mapped through the matrix log. Published rs-fMRI benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019) found this connectivity measure consistently the most predictive. It also tolerates all-zero ROIs better. The reference mean is fitted without labels on all items, and the classifier is unchanged, so only the connectivity measure differs.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol and ADHD prevalence. A pooled logistic regression on raw connectivity is likely spending its weights on site differences instead of the within-site signal that gets scored. I'm adding one change: before classification, each connectivity feature is centred and scaled within each acquisition site (a simple ComBat-style location/scale harmonization). Sites missing from the training fold fall back to their own label-free test statistics. I haven't run it, so I don't have a score for it yet.

Scanner and protocol differences between ADHD-200 sites are large. They shift the mean and scale of the connectivity edges, so one linear model trained on pooled data partly learns site differences instead of within-site ADHD effects. This change z-scores every edge within each site before the L2 logistic regression. It uses training-fold statistics per site and needs no labels. The goal is a better within-site AUROC.

I'm replacing the raw Pearson correlations with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrices, projected at the group geometric mean. This kind of connectome is consistently among the best for rs-fMRI classification, and it should be more stable than Pearson on the short, noisy ADHD-200 scans. The reference mean is computed without labels over all items inside `featurize`, so the classifier stays the same and only the connectivity measure changes.

Since scoring is within-site, I z-score each connectivity feature within each site before pooling. This label-free step uses each site's train and test items together and should leave the shared ADHD signal for the classifier.

Rescale the connectivity features within each site (centre and scale every edge using that site's subjects) before the global scaler and logistic regression. Scanner and protocol differences between sites are large, and the metric only compares subjects within a site. Removing those site-level offsets should let the regularized classifier learn from differences between subjects rather than differences between sites. The rescaling never uses labels; it pools each site's train and test subjects and falls back to global scaling when site information is missing. This is untested; I haven't run the harness, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Those shifts don't change the ranking inside a site, but they pull the logistic weights toward fitting site effects.
